Seminar Title:

Bridge Piers as Drivers of River Channel Evolution: Linking Hydraulics, Sediment Dynamics, and Morphological Change Across Scales

Abstract:

Bridge piers are essential components of river-crossing infrastructure, yet they substantially alter flow patterns and sediment transport processes, leading to local scour, downstream deposition, and long-term channel adjustments. While previous studies have investigated bridge-pier hydraulics, most have concentrated on localized scour around single pier configurations, leaving the combined hydro-morphodynamic and sedimentological effects of different pier geometries insufficiently understood. In addition, comprehensive assessments integrating remote sensing, laboratory experiments, field investigations, and hydraulic modelling remain limited. This study investigates the hydro-morphodynamic and sedimentological impacts of bridge piers on river channels using an integrated multi-scale framework. The research combines long-term satellite-based remote sensing, controlled laboratory experiments, field sedimentological analyses, and hydraulic modelling to examine flow alteration, sediment transport, channel adjustment, and river-bed evolution. Multi-temporal satellite imagery is used to quantify channel planform changes, erosion-accretion dynamics, sandbar development, and channel migration. Laboratory experiments conducted with three bridge pier geometries under controlled hydraulic conditions employ Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter measurements to characterize turbulence structures, velocity distributions, and their influence on scour and sediment transport. Field investigations validate experimental findings through measurements of channel geometry, hydraulic characteristics, and sedimentological properties under natural river conditions. Bed sediment samples collected upstream, adjacent to, and downstream of bridge piers are analysed for grain-size distribution and sorting characteristics to assess spatial variations in river-bed texture and depositional patterns. Experimental and field observations are subsequently integrated with hydraulic modelling to simulate bridge-induced hydro-morphodynamic processes under varying flow conditions and predict long-term channel responses. The findings will advance understanding of bridge pier geometry effects on river hydraulics, sediment dynamics, and channel evolution, providing scientific guidance for sustainable bridge design, river engineering, and infrastructure management. The framework supports improved assessment of future river changes.
